clue.text: Not to be confused with one of one's own

definitions.text: Not to be confused with one of one's own

parts.words: Not to be confused with one of one's own
parts.note: Virginia Woolf wrote both a novel named after a young man's lodging and the essay A Room of One's Own; the clue warns against mixing the two titles

explanation.surface: A warning not to mistake something for a thing of your own.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's 1922 novel shares the word for a chamber with her later feminist essay, so it is the other Woolf title with that word.

clue.text: Associated with ferret by Louisa M. Alcott?

definitions.text: Associated with ferret by Louisa M. Alcott?

parts.words: Associated with ferret by Louisa M. Alcott?
parts.note: a female ferret is called a jill, and Alcott wrote the novel ... and Jill, so the boy's name paired with that word in her title is wanted

explanation.surface: A question about Louisa M. Alcott writing about ferrets.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's novel title links the boy's name with Jill, which is also the term for a female ferret.

clue.text: Joyce the novelist

parts.note: not James Joyce but the Anglo-Irish novelist whose first name was Joyce, author of The Horse's Mouth

explanation.surface: A simple reference to a novelist called Joyce.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyone thinks of James Joyce; here Joyce is the first name, of the author of Mister Johnson and The Horse's Mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce Cary (1888-1957) was a novelist whose given name was Joyce.

clue.text: The Master's gin, for instance, from North Sea port, say

indicators.note: say signals that the port's name is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: Blyth is a port on the Northumberland coast of the North Sea
gin is an example of a spirit, a distilled drink

explanation.surface: Gin brought in by a notable figure from a North Sea harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Master' was Noel Coward's nickname, so the definition points at his play; Blyth is a Northumberland port, and the clue gives the drink before the port though the title runs the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward, known as the Master, wrote the 1941 comedy about a ghostly first wife, so the play is his.

clue.text: Early fifth columnist from Accra (habitual collaborator)

indicators.note: from tells us to take letters out of the run of words Accra habitual

explanation.surface: A traitor from Ghana's capital who habitually collaborated with the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Joshua, Rahab of Jericho hid the Israelite spies and helped them take the city; 'collaborator' in brackets repeats that idea. The run sits across 'Accra (habitual'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical woman sheltered enemy spies inside Jericho, an ancient example of a traitor within the walls.

clue.text: Our sly one, perhaps like Uriah Heep, may act in a troublesome way

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of our sly one could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Dickens's scheming Uriah Heep, our sly one, makes trouble when he acts.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep, the oily clerk of David Copperfield, fits 'Our sly one'; 'perhaps' rearranges those letters. 'like Uriah Heep, may act' is surface colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous means burdensome, so acting onerously is behaving in a way that weighs on or troubles others.

clue.text: Let it remain in Durrell's tetralogy

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the words Durrell's tetralogy

explanation.surface: Something kept intact in Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'Durrell's' starts the run, continuing into 'tetralogy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proofreader's mark, Latin for 'let it stand', tells the printer to keep a deleted word.

clue.text: Traditionally the best jokes in Wesker work

definitions.meaning: the saying goes that the familiar jokes are the best
Arnold Wesker wrote a 1972 play with this title about elderly Jewish Londoners

explanation.definitionFit: A proverb holds that well-worn jokes are the best, and Arnold Wesker used those words as a play title.

clue.text: "… an uncompromising girl whom none of them liked; a suspect of " (Evelyn Waugh)

definitions.text: "… an uncompromising girl whom none of them liked; a suspect of " (Evelyn Waugh)

parts.words: "… an uncompromising girl whom none of them liked; a suspect of " (Evelyn Waugh)
parts.note: the gap in the Waugh quotation is filled by the name of a left-wing political heresy

explanation.surface: A line from Evelyn Waugh describing a disliked girl with suspect politics.
explanation.definitionFit: In Waugh's line the girl is suspected of a revolutionary communist doctrine, the creed of Lenin's rival exiled in 1929.

clue.text: Vehicle Mr Frayn gives Woolf's eccentric intellectual

parts.note: Michael Frayn is the English playwright and novelist

explanation.surface: A playwright hands a car to an odd character in a Virginia Woolf novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Augustus Carmichael is the opium-taking poet who lounges on the lawn in To the Lighthouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus Carmichael, the dreamy poet in To the Lighthouse, is Woolf's odd scholarly guest.

clue.text: Bad mark for behaviour in Vigo film

definitions.text: Bad mark for behaviour in Vigo film

parts.words: Bad mark for behaviour in Vigo film
parts.note: Jean Vigo's 1933 boarding-school film is titled after the nought a French pupil scores for conduct

explanation.surface: A poor conduct grade awarded in a film by Jean Vigo.
explanation.walkthrough: Vigo's film is Zéro de conduite, nought for conduct, so the grid takes the number from its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Nought marks for conduct, the punishment in Vigo's boarding-school film, are the worst score possible.

clue.text: Bail out to describe dramatist with ailment

annotationWithheld.why: Bail out to describe dramatist with ailment: HOME (dramatist William Douglas Home) + SICKNESS (ailment) is plain, but no reading of 'Bail out to describe' accounts for letters without making 'ailment' do two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Bail out to describe dramatist with ailment

clue.text: 20's poem about the sun coming back at last?

definitions.text: 20's poem about the sun coming back at last?

parts.words: 20's poem about the sun coming back at last?
parts.note: 20 across is William Blake, and one of his prophetic books is named for a figure whose name is the Latin word for sun read backwards

explanation.surface: A question about a poem by 20 across concerning the sun's return.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's Los is SOL, the sun, turned around, so the title is fancifully a book about the sun coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's 1795 prophetic poem concerns Los, the creative spirit, whose name reverses the Latin for sun.

clue.text: Helper swam despairingly to reach one-legged sailor's quarry

indicators.note: swimming despairingly suggests thrashing about, so the letters of helper swam are churned

explanation.surface: A rescuer swam on in despair to reach a sailor's prey.
explanation.walkthrough: The one-legged sailor is Captain Ahab of Moby-Dick, whose quarry is the white whale.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahab, who lost a leg, hunts Moby Dick, a huge white cachalot.

clue.text: General name for playwright

definitions.meaning: Albert ... was a German field marshal of the Second World War
Joseph ... wrote the comedy Arsenic and Old Lace

explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to Hitler's field marshal Albert and to Joseph, the American dramatist of Arsenic and Old Lace.

clue.text: Akenside's were in the imagination

parts.note: Mark Akenside's long 1744 poem is titled after the delights of imagination

explanation.surface: A remark that the poet Akenside's somethings existed only in his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Akenside was an eighteenth-century poet and physician; his best-known work is The Pleasures of Imagination.
explanation.definitionFit: Akenside's poem names imaginative joys as delights of the mind.

clue.text: Dane's and Berger's Amazon units?

parts.note: Clemence Dane and Thomas Berger each wrote a novel called Regiment of Women, and companies of women soldiers are Amazon troops

explanation.surface: A question about formations of female warriors connected with two writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Military corps of women warriors would be Amazon troop bodies, echoing both novels titled Regiment of Women.

clue.text: "Thus in thy box Thou dost inclose us " (George Herbert)

definitions.text: "Thus in thy box Thou dost inclose us " (George Herbert)

parts.words: "Thus in thy box Thou dost inclose us " (George Herbert)
parts.note: the word missing from Herbert's line names the dark tropical hardwood of which the box, a coffin, is made

explanation.surface: A line by George Herbert about being shut in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert's line pictures a coffin of black tropical hardwood enclosing the dead.

clue.text: Wild evenings in Paris for Hall Caine protagonist

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of the French word run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: Raucous Parisian nights for a hero of Hall Caine's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Translate first: evenings in Paris are SOIRS, which 'Wild' rearranges. David Rossi is the revolutionary hero of Caine's The Eternal City.
explanation.definitionFit: David Rossi leads the story of The Eternal City, a bestselling 1901 novel by Hall Caine.

clue.text: Disgracefully rig survey of Simms work

indicators.note: rigging a survey disgracefully means fiddling it, so its letters are tampered with

explanation.surface: A scandal in which someone fixes an opinion poll.
explanation.walkthrough: William Gilmore Simms was a nineteenth-century South Carolina novelist; Guy Rivers (1834) was his first novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy Rivers is an 1834 border romance by the American author William Gilmore Simms.

clue.text: Wordsworth said that there was no doubt this poor man was mad

definitions.text: Wordsworth said that there was no doubt this poor man was mad

parts.words: Wordsworth said that there was no doubt this poor man was mad
parts.note: Wordsworth's remark about a visionary poet-engraver, whose madness he found more interesting than Byron's sanity

explanation.surface: A recollection of Wordsworth judging a fellow poet insane.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth reportedly said the author of Songs of Innocence was mad, yet more interesting than Lord Byron sane.

clue.text: Let first literary efforts add some excitement

indicators.note: first tells us to take the opening letter of each following word

explanation.surface: Allow early attempts at writing to bring a little thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let' is the verb to rent out, not to allow.
explanation.definitionFit: To let a flat is to rent it out under a contract, a synonym for leasing.

clue.text: Juliet and Romeo, both get instrument backing

annotationWithheld.why: Juliet and Romeo, both get instrument backing: the letters run backwards across 'Romeo, both' (EOBO), but 'Juliet and' and 'get' have no job in that reading, and no other parse accounts for them
annotationWithheld.clue: Juliet and Romeo, both get instrument backing

clue.text: Indian from Cumberland

parts.note: Richard Cumberland wrote the 1771 comedy The ... Indian, so the word before Indian in his title is wanted

explanation.surface: A person of Indian descent from the old English county of Cumberland.
explanation.walkthrough: Cumberland is a former county in north-west England, but here it is the dramatist Richard Cumberland.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Cumberland's comedy is The West Indian, so the compass point completes his title.

clue.text: Novelist familiarly known as author of Ravenshoe

definitions.text: Novelist familiarly known as author of Ravenshoe

parts.words: Novelist familiarly known as author of Ravenshoe
parts.note: Ravenshoe was written by Henry Kingsley, and the modern novelist whose first name is Kingsley is wanted

explanation.surface: A novelist known casually by the name of an old Victorian author.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley, surname of the Ravenshoe author, is the first name by which Kingsley Amis was familiarly called.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis's first name matches the surname of Henry Kingsley, so he is familiarly 'Kingsley'.

clue.text: Resembling As You Like It, or a piece by Beckett

definitions.meaning: a title meaning call it what you will refuses to give a name
Beckett's novel The Unnamable, third of his trilogy

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's offhand title leaves the play without a proper designation, and Beckett's 1953 novel takes that word as its name.

clue.text: It is therefore in Cartesian observation

definitions.text: It is therefore in Cartesian observation

parts.words: It is therefore in Cartesian observation
parts.note: Descartes's dictum cogito ... sum contains the Latin word for therefore

explanation.surface: Descartes's famous remark contains a therefore.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for therefore sits in Descartes's 'I think, therefore I am'.

clue.text: Evaluation of Modestine, perhaps, by some chaps at start of tour

annotationWithheld.why: Evaluation of Modestine, perhaps, by some chaps at start of tour: ASS (Modestine, Stevenson's donkey) + MEN + T are clear, but no clue word accounts for the ESS between them
annotationWithheld.clue: Evaluation of Modestine, perhaps, by some chaps at start of tour
